title: Honeybees: Tiny Workers
summary: How a honeybee colony shares its work, turns nectar into honey, pollinates plants, communicates with a dance, and helps farmers.
poll: Bees are more helpful than harmful to people.

versions.title: Bees at Work
versions.text:
See the bee on that flower? It is a honeybee. It is hard at work.

Bees live in a big group. The group is a colony. Its home is a hive. A hive can hold lots of bees.

Each hive has one queen. She lays the eggs. Most bees are workers. The workers are all female. They clean. They guard. They find food. A few bees are male. They are drones.

Bees sip a sweet juice from flowers. It is nectar. They take it home. They fan it with their wings. It gets thick. Now it is honey! Bees eat it when there are not many flowers.

Bees pick up a fine dust, too. It is pollen. It sticks to them. Some falls off on the next flower. That helps the plant make fruit and seeds.

A bee that finds good flowers does a dance. The dance tells the rest where to fly.

Farms need bees. Bees help crops like apples and nuts grow. In Saudi Arabia, bees make Sidr honey.

versions.title: Bees at Work
versions.text:
Look at a bee on a flower. It is busy. It is at work.

Bees live in a big group. The group is called a colony. A colony lives in a hive. One hive can have lots and lots of bees.

Each hive has one queen. She lays the eggs. Most bees are workers. All the workers are female. They clean, guard, and find food. A few bees are male. They are called drones.

Bees drink a sweet juice from flowers. It is called nectar. They take it back to the hive. They fan it with their wings. It gets thick. Now it is honey! Bees eat the honey when there are few flowers.

Bees also pick up a fine yellow dust. It is called pollen. It sticks to their legs. When a bee goes to the next flower, some pollen falls off. This helps the plant make fruit and seeds.

A bee that finds good flowers does a dance. The dance tells the other bees where to fly.

Farms need bees. Bees help crops like apples, melons, and nuts grow. In Saudi Arabia, bees make sweet Sidr honey.

versions.title: Honeybees: Busy Helpers
versions.text:
Look closely at a flower on a sunny day. You may see a honeybee at work. Bees are small, but they do big jobs.

Honeybees live in a big family called a colony. The colony makes its home in a hive. One hive can hold thousands and thousands of bees.

Every colony has one queen. Her job is to lay eggs. Most of the bees are workers. All the workers are female. They clean the hive, feed the young bees, guard the door, and find food. A few bees are male. They are called drones.

Bees drink a sweet juice from flowers. This juice is called nectar. The bees carry it back to the hive. They fan it with their wings until it gets thick. Then it is honey! The bees eat it when there are few flowers.

Bees also pick up a yellow dust called pollen. It sticks to their hairy legs and body. When a bee lands on the next flower, some pollen rubs off. This helps the plant make fruit and seeds.

When a bee finds good flowers, it does a dance in the hive. The dance shows the other bees which way to go and how far to fly.

Farms need bees. Bees help crops such as apples, melons, and almonds grow. In Saudi Arabia, people also enjoy honey made by bees, such as Sidr honey.

versions.title: Honeybees: Busy Helpers
versions.text:
On a bright morning, a honeybee may visit many flowers before it flies home. It may seem like a tiny insect with a tiny job. In fact, it belongs to one of the best teams in nature.

Honeybees live together in a large family called a colony. Their home is called a hive. A strong colony can have tens of thousands of bees, and each bee has a job.

The queen is the only bee that lays eggs. She can lay hundreds of eggs in one day. Worker bees are all female. They clean the hive, feed the young, build wax cells, guard the door, and collect food. Drones are the male bees. They do not collect food, and they cannot sting.

Worker bees drink nectar, a sweet liquid inside flowers. In the hive, they put the nectar into wax cells. Then they fan it with their wings to dry it out. Slowly, it turns into thick, sweet honey. The colony eats this honey when few flowers are in bloom.

As a bee feeds, yellow pollen sticks to its fuzzy body. Some of it rubs off on the next flower. This helps the plant make fruit and seeds.

When a bee finds good flowers, it does a special waggle dance. The dance tells other bees which way to fly and how far to go.

Farmers need bees to help many crops grow, such as apples, melons, and almonds. In Saudi Arabia, beekeepers in the southern mountains also collect Sidr honey.

versions.title: Honeybees: Tiny Workers
versions.text:
On a warm spring morning, a single honeybee may visit dozens of flowers before it returns home. It looks like a small insect doing a small job. But it is part of one of the most organized groups in nature.

Honeybees live together in a large family called a colony. A strong colony can hold tens of thousands of bees, and each one has a role. The queen is the only bee that lays eggs. She can lay hundreds in a single day. Worker bees are all female, and they do almost every other job. Young workers clean the wax cells, feed the babies, and build new comb. Older workers guard the door or fly out as foragers to collect food. Drones are the male bees. They do not collect food or sting. Their main job is to mate with a queen.

Foragers drink nectar, a sugary liquid found inside flowers. Back at the hive, the bees store the nectar in wax cells. They fan it with their wings until much of the water evaporates. The thick, sweet liquid that is left is honey. It feeds the colony when few flowers are blooming.

While a bee gathers food, yellow pollen sticks to its hairy body. Some of that pollen rubs off on the next flower. This movement of pollen is called pollination, and it lets plants make fruits and seeds.

When a forager finds a good patch of flowers, it does a waggle dance on the comb. The direction of the dance points the way. Its length shows how far to fly.

Farmers depend on this work. Many fruits, vegetables, and nuts need bees for pollination. Some farmers even rent hives and place them near their fields. In the mountains of southwestern Saudi Arabia, beekeepers also collect famous Sidr honey. It comes from bees that feed on the flowers of Sidr trees.

versions.title: Honeybees: Tiny Workers
versions.text:
On a warm spring morning, a single honeybee may visit dozens of flowers before it heads home. It seems like a tiny insect doing a tiny job. Yet each bee belongs to one of the most carefully organized communities in nature.

Honeybees live together in a large family called a colony. A healthy colony can include tens of thousands of bees, and every member has a particular role. The queen is the only bee that lays eggs. During the busy season, she may produce hundreds in a single day. Worker bees, which are all female, handle nearly every other task. Their jobs change as they grow older. Young workers clean cells and feed larvae. Middle-aged workers build wax comb and guard the entrance. The oldest workers become foragers that search for food. Drones, the male bees, cannot sting and do not gather food. Their main purpose is to mate with a young queen from another colony.

Foragers collect nectar, a sugary liquid made by flowers. Back in the hive, other workers spread the nectar into six-sided wax cells. They fan it with their wings until much of the water evaporates. The thick liquid that remains is honey. The colony stores it as food for times when few flowers are blooming.

As a forager moves among flowers, powdery pollen clings to its fuzzy body. Some of it rubs off on the next blossom. This process is called pollination, and it allows plants to form fruits and seeds.

When a forager discovers a rich patch of flowers, it returns and performs a waggle dance on the comb. The angle of the dance shows the direction, and the length of the waggling shows the distance.

Farmers rely on this work, since many fruits, vegetables, and nuts depend on pollination. Some farmers even rent hives and place them beside their fields. In southwestern Saudi Arabia, beekeepers in regions such as Al-Baha and Asir also produce prized Sidr honey.

The queen is the only bee that lays eggs, and in spring she may produce hundreds in a single day. Worker bees, all of them female, perform nearly every other task. Their duties change as they age. versions.title: Honeybees: Tiny Workers
versions.text:
On a warm spring morning, a single honeybee may visit dozens of flowers before returning to its hive. To a casual observer, it appears to be a tiny insect performing an unimportant chore. In reality, each bee belongs to one of the most remarkably organized communities in the natural world, and its daily labor helps feed millions of people.

Honeybees live in a large family known as a colony, which may contain tens of thousands of individuals during the productive season. Every member fulfills a specific function. The queen is the only bee that lays eggs, and at the height of spring she may deposit hundreds in a single day. Worker bees, all of them female, perform nearly every other responsibility. Their duties shift as they mature. Young workers clean cells and nourish the developing larvae; middle-aged workers produce wax, construct honeycomb, and defend the entrance. The oldest workers become foragers that venture outside to gather food. Drones, the male bees, possess no stinger and collect no food. Their principal purpose is to mate with a young queen from a different colony.

Foragers collect nectar, a sugary liquid that flowers produce to attract animal visitors. Inside the hive, other workers deposit the nectar in hexagonal wax cells. Then they fan it with their wings until most of the moisture evaporates. The concentrated liquid becomes honey, which the colony stores as an energy supply for periods when few flowers are blooming.

As a forager travels from blossom to blossom, powdery pollen clings to the fine hairs covering its body. Some of this pollen brushes off onto the next flower. This process, called pollination, enables many plants to develop fruits and seeds.

When a forager locates a valuable patch of flowers, it communicates the discovery through a waggle dance performed on the comb. The angle of the dance indicates the direction of the food in relation to the sun, while the duration of each waggle reveals the approximate distance.

Modern agriculture depends heavily on this activity, because numerous fruits, vegetables, and nuts require pollination. Some farmers even rent hives to position beside their orchards. In southwestern Saudi Arabia, beekeepers in regions such as Al-Baha and Asir also harvest highly valued Sidr honey from the blossoms of Sidr trees.

versions.title: Honeybees: Tiny Workers
versions.text:
On a warm spring morning, a single honeybee may visit dozens of flowers before returning to its hive. To a casual observer, it appears to be a tiny insect performing an insignificant chore. Yet each bee belongs to one of the most remarkably organized communities in the natural world, and its daily labor contributes to the food supply of millions of people.

Honeybees live in a large family known as a colony, which may contain tens of thousands of individuals during the productive season. Every member fulfills a specific function. The queen is the only bee that lays eggs, and at the height of spring she may deposit hundreds in a single day. Worker bees, all of them female, perform nearly every other responsibility, and their duties shift as they mature. Young workers clean cells and nourish developing larvae, middle-aged workers secrete wax and defend the entrance, and the oldest workers become foragers that venture outside to gather food. Drones, the male bees, possess no stinger and collect no food. Their principal purpose is to mate with a young queen from a different colony.

Foragers collect nectar, a sugary liquid that flowers produce to attract animal visitors, and carry it home in a special stomach. Along the way, the bees add enzymes that break down the sugars. Inside the hive, workers deposit the nectar in hexagonal wax cells and fan it with their wings until most of the moisture evaporates. Then they seal each cell with a cap of wax. The resulting honey serves as the colony's energy reserve during periods when few flowers are blooming.

As a forager travels from blossom to blossom, powdery pollen clings to the fine hairs covering its body. Some of this pollen brushes off onto the next flower, a process called pollination that enables many plants to develop fruits and seeds.

A forager that locates a valuable patch of flowers communicates the discovery through a waggle dance performed on the comb. The angle of the dance indicates the direction of the food in relation to the sun. The duration of each waggle reveals the approximate distance. The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch deciphered this language in the twentieth century and later shared a Nobel Prize for his research.

Modern agriculture depends heavily on these insects, since numerous fruits, vegetables, and nuts require pollination. Some farmers even rent hives to place beside their orchards. In southwestern Saudi Arabia, beekeepers in regions such as Al-Baha and Asir also harvest highly valued Sidr honey. Yet bees face serious threats, including pesticides, parasites such as mites, and the disappearance of wildflowers. That is why protecting them matters for everyone.

versions.title: Honeybees: Tiny Workers
versions.text:
On a temperate spring morning, a solitary honeybee may visit dozens of flowers before returning to its hive. To a casual observer, it appears to be an insignificant insect performing a trivial chore. Yet each bee belongs to one of the most sophisticated communities in the natural world, and its daily labor contributes substantially to the food supply of millions of people.

Honeybees live in a large, cooperative family known as a colony, which may contain tens of thousands of individuals during the productive season. Every member fulfills a specialized function. The queen is the only reproductive female, and at the height of spring she may deposit hundreds of eggs in a single day. Worker bees, all of them female, perform virtually every other responsibility, and their duties shift systematically as they mature. Younger workers clean cells and nourish developing larvae, middle-aged workers secrete wax and defend the entrance, and the oldest workers become foragers that venture outside to gather provisions. Drones, the male bees, possess no stinger and collect no food. Their principal purpose is to mate with a young queen from a different colony.

Foragers collect nectar, a sugary liquid that flowers manufacture to attract animal visitors, and transport it home in a specialized stomach. Throughout this process, the bees add enzymes that break complex sugars into simpler ones. Inside the hive, workers deposit the nectar in hexagonal wax cells and fan it with their wings until most of the moisture evaporates. Then they seal each cell beneath a protective cap of wax. The resulting honey functions as the colony's concentrated energy reserve during periods when few flowers are blooming.

As a forager travels from blossom to blossom, powdery pollen adheres to the dense hairs covering its body. Some of these grains brush off onto the next flower, a process called pollination that enables numerous plants to develop fruits and seeds.

A forager that locates a productive patch of flowers communicates the discovery through a waggle dance performed on the vertical surface of the comb. The angle of the dance indicates the direction of the food in relation to the sun, while the duration of each waggle reveals the approximate distance. The Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch deciphered this remarkable language during the twentieth century and subsequently shared a Nobel Prize for his investigations.

Contemporary agriculture depends considerably on these insects, because numerous fruits, vegetables, and nuts require pollination. Some farmers rent hives to position beside their orchards during flowering. In southwestern Saudi Arabia, beekeepers in mountainous regions such as Al-Baha and Asir also harvest highly valued Sidr honey. Nevertheless, bees confront serious threats, including pesticides, parasitic mites, and the disappearance of wildflowers, which explains why protecting them has become an international priority.

versions.title: Honeybees: Tiny Workers
versions.text:
On a temperate spring morning, a solitary honeybee may visit dozens of flowers before returning to its hive. To a casual observer, it appears to be an insignificant insect performing a trivial chore. In reality, each bee belongs to one of the most sophisticated communities in the natural world, and its seemingly modest labor contributes substantially to the agricultural food supply on which millions of people depend.

Honeybees inhabit a large, cooperative family known as a colony, which may contain tens of thousands of individuals during the productive season. Every member fulfills a specialized function. The queen is the colony's only reproductive female, and at the height of spring she may deposit hundreds of eggs in a single day. Worker bees, all of them female, perform virtually every other responsibility, and their duties shift systematically as they mature. Younger workers sanitize cells and nourish developing larvae, middle-aged workers secrete wax and defend the entrance, and the oldest workers become foragers that venture outside to gather provisions. Drones, the male bees, possess no stinger and collect no food, since their principal purpose is to mate with a young queen from a different colony.

Foragers collect nectar, a sugary liquid that flowers manufacture to attract animal visitors, and transport it home in a specialized stomach. Throughout this process, the bees introduce enzymes that convert complex sugars into simpler ones. Inside the hive, workers deposit the nectar in hexagonal wax cells and ventilate it with their wings until most of the moisture evaporates. Afterward, they seal each cell beneath a protective cap of wax. The resulting honey functions as the colony's concentrated energy reserve during periods when relatively few flowers are blooming.

As a forager travels from blossom to blossom, powdery pollen adheres to the dense, branched hairs covering its body, and some of these grains are inevitably transferred to the next flower. This process, called pollination, enables numerous plant species to fertilize their ovules and develop fruits and seeds.

A forager that locates a productive patch of flowers communicates the discovery to its sisters through a waggle dance performed on the vertical surface of the comb. The angle of the dance indicates the direction of the food in relation to the sun, while the duration of each waggle signals the approximate distance. The Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch deciphered this remarkable symbolic language during the twentieth century and subsequently shared a Nobel Prize for his investigations.

Contemporary agriculture depends considerably on these insects, because numerous fruits, vegetables, and nuts require pollination. Some farmers rent hives to position beside their orchards during the flowering period. In southwestern Saudi Arabia, beekeepers in mountainous regions such as Al-Baha and Asir also harvest highly valued Sidr honey. Nevertheless, honeybees confront serious environmental threats, including pesticides, parasitic mites, and the disappearance of wildflowers, which explains why their protection has become an international conservation priority.

versions.title: Honeybees: Tiny Workers
versions.text:
On a temperate spring morning, a solitary honeybee may visit dozens of flowers before returning to its hive. To a casual observer, it appears to be an insignificant insect performing a trivial chore. In reality, each bee belongs to one of the most sophisticated societies in the natural world, and its apparently modest labor contributes substantially to the agricultural productivity on which millions of people ultimately depend.

Honeybees inhabit an extensive, cooperative family known as a colony, which may comprise tens of thousands of individuals during the productive season, and every member performs a specialized function within an elaborate division of labor. The queen is the colony's only reproductive female, and at the height of spring she may deposit hundreds of eggs in a single day. Worker bees, all of them female, undertake virtually every remaining responsibility, and their duties evolve systematically as they mature. Younger workers sanitize cells and nourish developing larvae, middle-aged workers secrete wax and defend the entrance, and the oldest workers become foragers that venture into the surrounding landscape to gather provisions. Drones, the male bees, possess no stinger and collect no food, since their principal biological purpose is to mate with a young queen from a different colony.

Foragers collect nectar, a sugary liquid that flowers manufacture to attract animal visitors, and transport it home in a specialized stomach, introducing enzymes that convert complex sugars into simpler, more stable ones. Inside the hive, workers deposit the nectar in hexagonal wax cells and ventilate it with their wings until most of the moisture evaporates. Afterward, they seal each cell beneath a protective cap of wax. The resulting honey functions as the colony's concentrated energy reserve during periods when relatively few flowers are available.

As a forager travels from blossom to blossom, powdery pollen adheres to the dense, branched hairs covering its body, and some of these grains are inevitably transferred to subsequent flowers. This process, known as pollination, enables numerous plant species to fertilize their ovules and consequently develop fruits and seeds.

A forager that discovers a productive patch of flowers communicates its location to its sisters through a waggle dance performed on the vertical surface of the comb. The orientation of the dance indicates the direction of the food relative to the position of the sun, while the duration of each waggle signals the approximate distance. The Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch deciphered this extraordinary symbolic communication during the twentieth century and subsequently shared a Nobel Prize in recognition of his investigations.

Contemporary agriculture depends considerably on these industrious insects, because numerous fruits, vegetables, and nuts require pollination, and some commercial growers rent hives to position beside their orchards throughout the flowering period. In southwestern Saudi Arabia, beekeepers in mountainous regions such as Al-Baha and Asir also harvest highly valued Sidr honey. Nevertheless, honeybees confront considerable environmental pressures, including pesticides, parasitic mites, and the progressive disappearance of wildflowers, which explains why their protection has become an international conservation priority.

The butterfly drank nectar from a red flower.

keyWords.definition: a fine yellow powder made by flowers

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to keep bees away from a picnic
How honeybees live, work, and help plants and people
Why honey is the only food bees eat
How bees sleep in their hive at night
questions.why: Every part of the article tells how bees live in a colony, do jobs, make honey, and help plants and farms.

wrong.A: The article never talks about picnics or keeping bees away.
wrong.C: Honey is one part of the article, but it is not the whole topic.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about how bees sleep.

questions.stem: Which bee lays the eggs in a colony?
options: The drones
The worker bees
Every bee in the hive
The queen
questions.why: The article says each hive has one queen, and she lays the eggs.

wrong.A: Drones are the male bees. They do not lay eggs.
wrong.B: Workers clean, guard, and find food, but the article says the queen lays the eggs.
wrong.C: Only one bee, the queen, lays the eggs.

questions.stem: What do bees make honey from?
options: Nectar from flowers
Pollen on their legs
Water from a river
Wax from the hive
questions.why: Bees drink nectar, carry it to the hive, and fan it until it becomes thick honey.

wrong.B: Pollen sticks to bees and helps plants make seeds, but honey comes from nectar.
wrong.C: The article does not say honey is made from river water.
wrong.D: Wax is used to build cells, not to make honey.

questions.stem: What does the word pollen mean in this article?
options: A sweet juice inside flowers
A group of bees that live together
A powder that flowers make
A dance that bees do
questions.why: The article describes pollen as a fine yellow dust that comes from flowers and sticks to bees.

wrong.A: A sweet juice inside flowers is nectar, not pollen.
wrong.B: A group of bees that live together is a colony.
wrong.D: The dance is how bees share where flowers are. It is not pollen.

questions.stem: What happens when pollen from one flower rubs off on the next flower?
options: The plant can make fruit and seeds.
The bee forgets the way home.
The flower turns nectar into honey.
The hive gets a new queen.
questions.why: The article explains that when pollen falls off on the next flower, it helps the plant make fruit and seeds.

wrong.B: The article says nothing about bees getting lost.
wrong.C: Bees make honey inside the hive, not flowers.
wrong.D: Pollen on flowers has nothing to do with a new queen.

questions.stem: Why would a farmer most likely be happy to have bees near the farm?
options: Bees eat the bugs that hurt plants.
Bees keep birds away from the trees.
Bees make the soil wet.
Bees help the crops make fruit.
questions.why: The article says bees move pollen so plants can make fruit, and that farms need bees for crops like apples and melons.

wrong.A: The article does not say bees eat other bugs.
wrong.B: Nothing in the article says bees scare birds.
wrong.C: Bees do not water the soil.

questions.stem: Why does a hive need so many worker bees?
options: Workers are the only bees that lay eggs.
There are many jobs for them to do.
They must keep the drones awake.
Each worker lives in its own hive.
questions.why: Workers clean, guard, and find food. So many tasks need many bees.

wrong.A: The queen lays the eggs, not the workers.
wrong.C: The article does not say workers keep drones awake.
wrong.D: All the bees in a colony live together in one hive.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article by talking about farms?
options: To teach readers how to grow apples
To show that bees can be dangerous
To show why bees matter to people
To explain how honey is sold in shops
questions.why: The ending shows that bees help farm crops grow and give us honey, so they matter to people.

wrong.A: The article names apples but does not teach how to grow them.
wrong.B: The ending is about how bees help, not how they can hurt.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about selling honey in shops.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Drones are the most important bees because they mate with queens.
Honey is made only in the mountains of Saudi Arabia.
Honeybees work as a team that helps plants and farms.
Bees are dangerous insects that people should avoid.
questions.why: The article explains how the colony shares jobs, makes honey, pollinates plants, and supports farming.

wrong.A: Drones are mentioned, but the article does not say they are the most important bees.
wrong.B: Sidr honey is one example; bees make honey in many places.
wrong.D: The article shows that bees are helpful, not that people should avoid them.

questions.stem: According to the article, how do a worker bee's jobs change as it gets older?
options: It starts with jobs inside the hive and later flies out to find food.
It begins as a forager and later becomes a queen.
It guards the entrance for its whole life.
It turns into a drone when it is old.
questions.why: Young workers clean cells and feed young bees; older workers guard the hive or become foragers.

wrong.B: Workers do not become queens, and foraging comes later in life, not first.
wrong.C: Guarding is only one stage of a worker's life.
wrong.D: Workers are female and never turn into drones, which are male.

questions.stem: What does the direction of the waggle dance tell the other bees?
options: How much honey is stored
How far away the food is
Which bees should stay home
Which way to fly to the food
questions.why: The article says the direction or angle of the dance points the way to the flowers.

wrong.B: Distance is shown by the length of the waggle, not its direction.
wrong.C: The dance does not assign jobs to bees.

questions.stem: The bees fan the nectar with their wings until water evaporates. What does evaporates mean?
options: Freezes into ice
Turns into a gas and leaves
Mixes with pollen
Drips out of the cell
questions.why: When water evaporates, it changes into vapor and goes into the air, so the nectar becomes thicker.

wrong.A: Fanning moves warm air; it does not freeze the nectar.
wrong.C: Pollen is not part of this step of making honey.
wrong.D: The water leaves as vapor, not by dripping, and the article says the liquid becomes thick.

questions.stem: Why is pollination important to plants?
options: It gives plants the water they need.
It keeps insects away from the leaves.
It lets plants make seeds and fruit.
It turns nectar into honey.
questions.why: The article explains that moving pollen between flowers lets plants form fruits and seeds.

wrong.B: Pollination actually depends on insects visiting flowers.
wrong.D: Bees turn nectar into honey inside the hive; that is not pollination.

questions.stem: Based on the article, what would most likely happen on an apple farm if all the bees disappeared?
options: The trees would produce fewer apples.
The apples would become sweeter.
The trees would make more nectar.
The farm would produce more honey.
questions.why: Fruit crops need bees for pollination, so without bees, fewer flowers would become apples.

wrong.B: Nothing in the article links bees to sweeter apples.
wrong.C: The article does not say trees make more nectar without bees.
wrong.D: Honey comes from bees, so there would be less honey, not more.

questions.stem: What does the waggle dance suggest about honeybees?
options: They dance to keep the hive warm.
They are afraid of flying far away.
They only visit flowers they can see from the hive.
They can share information.
questions.why: A forager uses the dance to tell other bees where food is, which shows that bees communicate.

wrong.A: The article says the dance shows where food is, not that it warms the hive.
wrong.B: The dance shows bees fly to distant flowers, so they are not afraid to.
wrong.C: The dance helps bees find flowers they cannot see from the hive.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the article?
options: As a story told by one bee, from morning to night
By describing the colony, then how bees make honey and pollinate, then why they matter
By comparing honeybees with other insects
By listing problems with bees and then solutions
questions.why: The article moves from the colony's members, to honey and pollination, to the dance, and ends with farms and Saudi honey.

wrong.A: The article is not told by a bee and does not follow one day.
wrong.C: Honeybees are not compared with other insects.
wrong.D: The article mostly explains how bees work; it is not organized around problems and solutions.

MID.prompt: Explain why farmers depend on honeybees. Use at least two details from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I supported my answer with at least two details from the article.
I explained how each detail connects to farming.

keyWords.definition: a natural substance in living things that speeds up a chemical change
keyWords.example: An enzyme in your saliva starts breaking down bread while you chew.

keyWords.definition: the transfer of pollen between flowers so that plants can produce seeds
keyWords.example: Many desert plants rely on insects and wind for pollination.

keyWords.definition: an animal that searches an area for food
keyWords.example: The fox is a clever forager that hunts at night.

keyWords.definition: to change from a liquid into a vapor
keyWords.example: Seawater left in shallow pools will evaporate and leave salt behind.

keyWords.definition: to share information or ideas with others
keyWords.example: Dolphins communicate with clicks and whistles.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Karl von Frisch was the most important scientist of the twentieth century.
Honey is valuable mainly because it is produced in Saudi Arabia.
Pesticides have caused farmers to stop using honeybees.
Honeybees form a highly organized society whose work sustains plants and agriculture.
questions.why: The article describes the colony's division of labor, honey-making, pollination, and communication, and explains their importance to farming.

wrong.A: Von Frisch is a supporting detail about the waggle dance, and the article makes no such claim.
wrong.B: Sidr honey is one regional example, not the main point.
wrong.C: The article lists pesticides as a threat but says farmers still rent hives.

questions.stem: According to the article, what do bees add to nectar that breaks down its sugars?
options: Pollen
Enzymes
Wax
Water
questions.why: The article states that bees add enzymes that break complex sugars into simpler ones.

wrong.A: Pollen is carried on the bee's body; it does not break down sugars.
wrong.C: Wax is used to build cells and cap them.
wrong.D: Bees remove water from nectar; they do not add it.

questions.stem: Which threat to honeybees does the article mention?
options: Cold desert winters
Too many wildflowers
Parasites such as mites
Competition from drones
questions.why: The final paragraph lists pesticides, parasites such as mites, and the loss of wildflowers.

wrong.A: The article does not mention cold winters as a threat.
wrong.B: The article says the disappearance of wildflowers is a threat, not too many.
wrong.D: Drones are part of the colony, not a threat to it.

questions.stem: The article says Karl von Frisch deciphered the bees' dance. What does deciphered mean?
options: Figured out the meaning of
Invented a new form of
Copied and performed
Prevented or stopped
questions.why: Von Frisch worked out what the dance means, which is why he was honored for his research.

wrong.B: Bees created the dance; von Frisch did not invent it.
wrong.C: He studied the dance; he did not perform it.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests he stopped the bees from dancing.

questions.stem: Why do worker bees fan the nectar with their wings?
options: To cool the queen
To spread pollen through the hive
To attract drones from other colonies
To remove water from it
questions.why: Fanning makes the moisture evaporate, which concentrates the nectar into honey.

wrong.A: The article links fanning to nectar, not to the queen.
wrong.B: Pollen is not mentioned in the honey-making step.
wrong.C: Drones are not connected to fanning in the article.

questions.stem: Why would farmers most likely rent hives to place beside their orchards?
options: To sell the honey for a high price
To keep pests away from their trees
To make sure their crops are pollinated
To teach bees how to dance
questions.why: Fruit and nut crops need pollination, so farmers bring bees to their orchards to make sure the flowers are pollinated.

wrong.A: The article connects renting hives to pollination, not to selling honey.
wrong.B: Bees are not described as protecting trees from pests.
wrong.D: The waggle dance is natural; it is not taught by people.

questions.stem: The dance shows direction in relation to the sun. What can be inferred from this detail?
options: Bees can use the sun's position to navigate.
Bees fly only at noon.
Bees perform the dance outside the hive.
Bees cannot see flowers clearly.
questions.why: If the dance uses the sun as a reference point, foragers must be able to use the sun to find their way.

wrong.B: The detail does not limit flying to a particular time.
wrong.C: The article says the dance is performed on the comb, inside the hive.
wrong.D: The article says nothing about bees' eyesight.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with the threats that honeybees face?
options: To argue that people should stop eating honey
To show why protecting bees matters
To explain how honey is stored
To compare bees with other pollinators
questions.why: After showing how valuable bees are, the author lists dangers to explain why their protection is a priority.

wrong.A: The article never suggests that people stop eating honey.
wrong.C: Honey storage is explained earlier, not at the end.
wrong.D: No other pollinators are compared in the article.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say honeybees are more valuable for pollination than for honey. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
